# Abstract

This study reconstructs the long-term demographic evolution, spatial distribution and settlement hierarchy of Central Asia from the onset of the nomadic Iron Age in 1000BC to the reconfiguration of late antiquity in 500AD. Encompassing 3.890.946 km² across nine physiographic territories, aggregate domain population expanded from 1,45M (1.450.000) in 1000BC to 2,2M (2.200.000) under Achaemenid imperial consolidation in 500BC, climbed to 2,75M (2.750.000) during the Hellenistic Greco-Bactrian horizon in 200BC, and achieved a classical antiquity apex of 3,75M (3.750.000) in 200AD under the Kushan Empire, Parthian Margiana and the Kangju confederation [@Morris2021Economic; @Morris2023Political; @Grenet2025Histoire]. This civilisational apex was anchored by sophisticated gravity-fed irrigation networks along the Zeravshan, Murghab, Surkhandarya, Amu Darya and Syr Darya deltas, supporting intensive double-cropping, viticulture and sprawling walled metropolises [@MirMakhamad2024Agricultur; @MirMakhamad2023Testing; @Dhawi2024Oasis]. Following third-century political fragmentation, Roman-Sasanian pressures and early Hunnic-Kidarite nomadic incursions, domain population contracted to 3,35M in 350AD before undergoing an early mediaeval recovery to 3,55M (3.550.000) by 500AD under Hephthalite stability and expanding Sogdian mercantile networks [@Grenet2025Histoire; @Franklin2023Archaeolog]. Demographically, Sogdiana formed the primary core, growing from 304,5k in 1000BC to 787,5k at its peak and 745,5k in 500AD, complemented by Dayuan Ferghana and Kangju Chach (637,5k peak; 603,5k in 500AD), Parthian Margiana (487,5k peak) and Northern Bactria (450k peak) [@Morris2021Economic; @BETTS2016Akchakhan]. Calibrated across 442 domestic catchments using non-stationary Matérn kriging ($\nu = 3/2$, $\tau_1 = 1,5$, $\tau_2 = 2,775$), the empirical register integrates 917 catalogued settlements led by Merv (60.000), Samarkand (45.000), Old Termez (38.000), Bukhara (35.000), Old Nisa (24.000), Tashkent (22.000), Kunya-Urgench (22.000) and Erkurgan (18.000) [@Sanahuja2020Historiogr; @Armaroli2026Tracing].

# Background

## Environmental Setting and the Hydro-Ecological Oasis Triad

The arid and semi-arid terrain of Central Asia is characterised by a structural dichotomy between hyper-arid desert basins (the Karakum and Kyzylkum), vast semi-arid steppes extending north of the Syr Darya into the Kazakh uplands, and high glaciated mountain systems (the Pamir, Tian Shan, Hindu Kush and Kopet Dag) [@Librado2024Widespread; @Namen2025Human]. In this endorheic continental environment, human settlement has historically depended on an ecological triad consisting of piedmont alluvial fans, riverine oasis corridors and seasonal steppe pasturelands [@MirMakhamad2024Agricultur; @Franklin2023Archaeolog].

Mountain glaciers and seasonal snowpack provide the primary hydrological engine of the domain, feeding major arterial streams: the Amu Darya (ancient Oxus), the Syr Darya (ancient Jaxartes), the Zeravshan (ancient Polytimetos), the Murghab (ancient Margos), the Tedzhen (ancient Hari Rud) and the Surkhandarya [@MirMakhamad2024Agricultur; @Sanahuja2020Historiogr]. Where these rivers emerge from mountain gorges onto foothill plains, they discharge extensive alluvial fans whose fertile loessic soils and accessible groundwater table facilitated early irrigation agriculture [@Dhawi2024Oasis; @MirMakhamad2023Testing]. 

Throughout the first millennium BC, human communities perfected sophisticated hydraulic techniques, including deep mainline diversion canals, radial distribution ditches, sluice gates and subterranean infiltration channels (*karez* or *qanat*) along the Kopet Dag piedmont [@Dhawi2024Oasis; @Morris2021Economic]. These systems converted inhospitable desert margins into lush agrarian archipelagos capable of supporting dense nucleated populations, orchard arboriculture, cotton, pulses and double-cropped cereals [@MirMakhamad2023Testing; @MirMakhamad2023Food]. Concurrently, interfluvial desert expanses and peripheral grasslands remained the domain of mobile pastoralists whose seasonal transhumance routes linked lowland winter refugia with alpine summer pastures [@Librado2024Widespread; @Armaroli2026Tracing].

## The Scythian-Saka Nomadic Horizon and Steppe Pastoralism

During the early first millennium BC, the expansion of equestrian pastoral nomadism fundamentally reorganised the steppe and highland zones of Central Asia [@Librado2024Widespread; @SENGUL2024Origin]. Known collectively to Classical Greek authors as Scythians and to Achaemenid Old Persian inscriptions as Saka (*Sakā*), these eastern Iranian-speaking pastoral confederations perfected mounted archery, composite bow technology, specialised horse tack and lightweight felt dwellings suitable for rapid overland movement [@Librado2024Widespread; @Zairova2026Phenomenon; @SENGUL2024Origin].

Achaemenid royal inscriptions, notably Darius I's monumental relief at Behistun and the Persepolis tribute lists, distinguished three primary Saka branches within and adjacent to the imperial frontier: the *Sakā paradraya* (Saka across the water, bordering the Aral and Black seas), the *Sakā tigraxaudā* (pointed-hat Saka, occupying the Semirechye and Tian Shan corridors), and the *Sakā haumavargā* (haoma-drinking Saka, located in the Pamir and Badakhshan highlands) [@SENGUL2024Origin; @Grenet2025Histoire]. Further west and northwest across the trans-Caspian steppe roamed the warlike Massagetae and Dahae confederations, whose mobile pastoral strategies exploited the seasonal pasture cycles between the Caspian Sea, the Ust-Urt plateau and the lower Syr Darya [@Cinar2026Kazakh; @SENGUL2024Origin].

Archaeologically, the Saka horizon is distinguished by monumental kurgan burial mounds containing exquisite gold, bronze and iron artefacts rendered in the dynamic Eurasian Animal Style, as exemplified by the royal burials of Issyk in Semirechye, Tasmola in the central Kazakh steppe and the Altai mortuary complexes [@Zairova2026Phenomenon; @Anon2026; @Mallick2024Allen]. Genomic and isotopic analyses demonstrate that these steppe communities maintained continuous biological and material exchange with settled oasis populations, trading horses, livestock, hides and wool for agricultural grain, manufactured metals, wine and luxury textiles [@Mallick2024Allen; @Armaroli2026Tracing; @Librado2024Widespread]. Rather than existing in perpetual conflict, mobile pastoralists and sedentary oasis farmers formed an interdependent, co-evolutionary socio-economic continuum [@Franklin2023Archaeolog; @Morris2021Economic].

## Achaemenid Integration and Imperial Satrapal Infrastructure

Between 550BC and 530BC, Cyrus the Great incorporated the historic lands of Bactria, Sogdiana, Margiana, Parthia and Chorasmia into the Achaemenid Persian Empire, meeting his death on the northeastern frontier in battle against Tomyris and the Massagetae near the lower Syr Darya [@SENGUL2024Origin; @Grenet2025Histoire]. Under Darius I (522BC to 486BC), the region was systematically organised into satrapies responsible for substantial annual silver tributes, military levies and elite cavalry contingents [@Morris2023Political; @Morris2023Economic].

Imperial integration exerted a profound transformative effect upon the Central Asian landscape [@Morris2021Economic; @BETTS2016Akchakhan]. Royal administrative centres were founded or expanded, including Marakanda (Afrasiab/Samarkand), Bactra (Zariaspa/Balkh), Merv (Gyaur Kala) and Cyropolis along the Syr Darya [@Grenet2025Histoire; @Sanahuja2020Historiogr]. Achaemenid engineers and satrapal governors coordinated massive public works projects, including the construction of grand trunk canals that substantially increased arable acreage in the Zeravshan and Murghab basins [@Dhawi2024Oasis; @MirMakhamad2024Agricultur]. 

In Classical Khwarazm, downstream along the lower Amu Darya delta, monumental mudbrick fortresses and palaces such as Akchakhan-kala and early phases of Toprak-Kala and Koy-Krylgan-Kala arose during this era [@BETTS2016Akchakhan]. Wall paintings and architectural remains from Akchakhan-kala reveal complex Zoroastrian religious iconography, dynastic cults and high artistic craftsmanship sustained by surplus oasis agriculture [@BETTS2016Akchakhan; @Grenet2025Histoire]. By 500BC, satrapal infrastructure, pacified trade corridors and hydraulic expansion had lifted domain population to 2,2M people, establishing an enduring urban and agrarian framework across Central Asia [@Morris2021Economic; @Morris2023Economic].

## Hellenistic Foundations: The Greco-Bactrian and Indo-Greek Kingdoms

Alexander the Great's campaigns between 329BC and 327BC shattered Achaemenid satrapal rule but met fierce regional resistance in Sogdiana and Bactria, led by Spitamenes and local mountain chieftains [@Sanahuja2020Historiogr; @Grenet2025Histoire]. To pacify the region, Alexander established a chain of fortified Greek garrison colonies, including Alexandria the Furthest (Alexandria Eschate, modern Khujand) on the Syr Darya and Alexandria on the Oxus (Ai Khanoum) in eastern Bactria [@Sanahuja2020Historiogr; @Francfort2020Quelques]. Alexander's marriage to Roxana, daughter of the Sogdian nobleman Oxyartes, symbolised the synthesis of Macedonian military elites with indigenous Iranian nobility [@Grenet2025Histoire; @Fariello2024Battriana].

Following the partition of Alexander's empire, Central Asia fell to Seleucus I Nicator and Antiochus I Soter, who fortified Merv as Antiochia Margiana and established royal mints [@Morris2021Economic; @Sanahuja2020Historiogr]. Around 250BC, the Seleucid satrap Diodotus I declared independence, founding the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom, while further west in Parthia, Arsaces I united the Parni pastoralists to establish the Arsacid Parthian Empire along the Kopet Dag foothills, anchoring his capital at Nisa [@Morris2021Economic; @Morris2023Political].

The Greco-Bactrian Kingdom (c. 250BC to 130BC), especially under Demetrius I, Eucratides I and Menander I, represented a flourishing apex of Hellenistic urbanism and monetary economy in Central Asia [@Sanahuja2020Historiogr; @Francfort2020Quelques; @Morris2021Economicb]. Cities featured classical Greek architectural elements, including colonnaded gymnasia, theatres, Corinthian capitals, administrative archives written on papyrus and parchment in Greek script, and bronze and silver coinage of extraordinary artistic fidelity [@Francfort2020Quelques; @Morris2021Economicb]. Hellenistic urban centres such as Old Termez (Demetrias) and Takht-i Sangin on the upper Oxus operated as bustling cosmopolitan hubs linking Mediterranean trade with India and China [@Sanahuja2020Historiogr; @Fariello2024Battriana; @Franklin2023Archaeolog].

## The Kushan Hegemony and Classical Urban Climax

During the late second century BC, nomadic migrations originating in northwestern China triggered profound geopolitical shifts across the Central Asian steppe [@Zhang2023Characteri; @Fariello2024Battriana]. The Da Yuezhi confederation, displaced by the Xiongnu, migrated westward across the Ili and Ferghana basins, pushing the Saka into Bactria and Drangiana (Sakastan) and ultimately overthrowing Greek dynastic rule in Bactria around 130BC [@Fariello2024Battriana; @Zhang2023Characteri; @Morris2021Economic].

Within a century, one of the five principal Yuezhi clans, the Guishuang (*Kushanas*), united the confederation under Kujula Kadphises to establish the Kushan Empire [@Morris2021Economic; @Morris2023Political]. Under Kanishka I (c. 127AD to 150AD) and his successors Huvishka and Vasudeva I, the Kushan Empire expanded from its northern Bactrian and Tokharistan heartlands into Gandhara, Mathura and the Gangetic plain, creating an imperial polity that bridged Central Asia and northern India [@Morris2021Economic; @Grenet2025Histoire].

The Kushan period witnessed unprecedented demographic and commercial expansion [@Morris2021Economic; @Franklin2023Archaeolog]. As masters of the overland Silk Road, Kushan rulers protected trade caravans transporting Chinese silk, Roman glass, Indian spices and Central Asian lapis lazuli and horses [@Franklin2023Archaeolog; @Zhang2023Characteri; @Wang2022Revealing]. Kushan urbanism attained historic dimensions at sites such as Dalverzin-Tepe, Old Termez, Khalchayan and Takht-i Sangin, where Buddhist monasteries (*viharas*) and stupas coexisted harmoniously with Zoroastrian dynastic fire temples and Hellenistic artistic traditions [@Francfort2020Quelques; @Morris2021Economic; @Grenet2025Histoire]. In 200AD, domain population reached its classical maximum of 3,75M people, sustained by an exceptionally integrated trans-Eurasian trade network and intensive oasis agriculture [@Morris2021Economic; @MirMakhamad2024Agricultur].

## Regional Trajectories: Khwarazm, Kangju and Dayuan

Beyond the formal frontiers of the Kushan Empire, autonomous oasis kingdoms and nomadic confederations flourished along the northern and western axes [@BETTS2016Akchakhan; @Zhang2023Characteri]. In the lower Amu Darya delta, the Classical Khwarazmian state reached its cultural zenith under the local Afrighid dynasty [@BETTS2016Akchakhan]. Toprak-Kala served as a grand royal residential citadel containing elaborate multi-roomed palace complexes, aristocratic archives inscribed on wood and leather in Khwarazmian Aramaic script, and magnificent wall murals depicting dynastic hunts and musicians [@BETTS2016Akchakhan]. Nearby, Koy-Krylgan-Kala functioned as an enigmatic circular fortress-temple dedicated to royal funerary rituals and astronomical observations [@BETTS2016Akchakhan].

In the middle Syr Darya and Chach (Tashkent) oasis, the powerful Kangju (*Kangju*) confederation established a strategic dominion that controlled vital northern trade routes linking China, the Altai and western Eurasia [@Zhang2023Characteri; @Cinar2026Kazakh]. Anchored by the major fortified metropolis of Kanka in the Tashkent oasis and the extensive fortified mudbrick settlements of the Jety-Asar culture along the dry palaeo-channels of the Syr Darya, Kangju maintained a potent military force capable of challenging both the Kushans and the Han Empire [@Zhang2023Characteri; @Anon2026].

In the fertile intermontane basin of the upper Syr Darya, the state of Dayuan (Ferghana) flourished as an independent, densely urbanised realm celebrated for its walled cities, viticulture, alfalfa cultivation and legendary "heavenly horses" (*tianma*) [@Zhang2023Characteri; @Fariello2024Battriana]. The expedition of Han General Li Guangli in 101BC against the Dayuan capital of Ershi (Marhamat/Ura-Tyube) highlighted the strategic value of Ferghana's equestrian resources and opened regular diplomatic and mercantile intercourse between China and Central Asian oasis polities [@Zhang2023Characteri; @Franklin2023Archaeolog].

# Methodology

## Territorial Partition and Analytical Units

To reconstruct demographic densities without geographic distortion across the disparate biomes of Central Asia, this study partitions the domain into nine territorial and biophysical units encompassing 3.890.946 km² across 65.332 five-arcminute grid cells (Table \ref{tab:regions-scythian}):

1. Parthian Kopet Dag and Margiana Oasis (388.334 km²): Encompassing the piedmont slope of southern Turkmenistan, the Murghab delta (Merv) and the Tedzhen alluvial fan.
2. Classical Khwarazm Oasis State (332.485 km²): Encompassing the lower Amu Darya delta, the Sarykamysh basin and adjacent Aral shores.
3. Sogdiana Core (123.360 km²): Encompassing the Zeravshan and Qashqadarya river valleys (Samarkand, Bukhara, Kesh/Shahrisabz, Erkurgan and Panjikent).
4. Northern Bactria and Upper Oxus (130.455 km²): Encompassing Tokharistan, the Surkhandarya, Kafirnigan and Vakhsh valleys (Old Termez, Dalverzin-Tepe and Takht-i Sangin).
5. Pamir and Badakhshan Saka Highlands (39.421 km²): Encompassing high-altitude montane valleys and pastoral corridors of eastern Tajikistan.
6. Dayuan Ferghana and Kangju Chach-Middle Syr Darya (405.248 km²): Encompassing the Ferghana intermontane basin, the Tashkent oasis (Chach) and the middle Syr Darya (Otrar).
7. Semirechye and Tian Shan Saka-Wusun Corridor (377.744 km²): Encompassing the Chu, Talas and Ili river valleys, Lake Issyk-Kul and the northern slopes of the Tian Shan.
8. Aral-Caspian Massagetae and Sarmatian Western Steppe (791.785 km²): Encompassing the desert-steppe expanses between the Caspian Sea, the Aral Sea and the Emba River.
9. Tasmola-Saka Central and Northern Kazakh Steppe (1.302.114 km²): Encompassing the extensive semi-arid grassland plateau of central and northern Kazakhstan.

At each historical benchmark year $t \in \{-1000, -500, -200, 1, 200, 350, 500\}$, total regional population $P_r(t)$ synthesises archaeological site counts, architectural habitational multipliers, and pastoral carrying-capacity envelopes [@Morris2021Economic; @MirMakhamad2024Agricultur]:

$$P_r(t) = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{S}_r} A_k(t) \cdot \delta_k(t) + \mathcal{H}_r(t) \cdot \rho_r(t)$$

where $A_k(t)$ is the fortified intramural area of settlement $k$, $\delta_k(t)$ represents the urban residential density (calibrated between 120 and 220 persons per hectare for mudbrick multi-room compounds), $\mathcal{H}_r(t)$ denotes the estimated rural and pastoral household count, and $\rho_r(t)$ is the mean family multiplier (5 to 5,5 persons per domestic unit) [@Morris2021Economic; @BETTS2016Akchakhan; @Armaroli2026Tracing].

## Archaeological Settlement Aggregation and Multi-Proxy Calibration

Calibrating demographic headcounts requires harmonising diverse archaeological datasets across five contemporary Central Asian republics [@Anon2026Reflecting; @Franklin2023Archaeolog]. The spatial catalogue integrates 917 primary settlements compiled from comprehensive excavation registers, including the Central Asian Archaeological Landscapes (CAAL) database, Al-Thurayya historical gazetteer, Pleiades Classical antiquity compendium, and national heritage registries [@Franklin2023Archaeolog; @Sanahuja2020Historiogr].

Each settlement is assigned geocoded WGS84 coordinates, documented chronological horizons, fortified area measurements and estimated population spans [@Sanahuja2020Historiogr; @BETTS2016Akchakhan]. To avoid contemporaneity over-counting, multi-period sites are adjusted using stratigraphic phase durations and radiocarbon summed probability distributions [@MirMakhamad2024Agricultur; @Namen2025Human]. Rural populations in irrigated oasis belts are calibrated based on canal discharge capacities, estimated crop yields (wheat, barley, foxtail millet, rice, grapes) and historical land-tenure patterns [@MirMakhamad2024Agricultur; @MirMakhamad2023Testing; @Dhawi2024Oasis]. In pastoral zones, population ceilings are constrained by livestock herd biomass requirements and seasonal grazing ranges [@Librado2024Widespread; @Armaroli2026Tracing].

## Spatial Kriging and Biophysical Covariates

Spatial population allocation across the domain is modelled via the regional kriging framework, integrating 12.473 domestic assigned records across 442 domestic catchments (with 396 active domestic catchments covering 51.089 active raster cells out of 65.332 valid domain cells) [@Franklin2023Archaeolog; @Mallick2024Allen]. Residual spatial dependence is estimated using Paciorek-Schervish non-stationary Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) covariance functions:

$$C(s_i, s_j) = \sigma_i \sigma_j \, |\Sigma_i|^{1/4} |\Sigma_j|^{1/4} \left|\frac{\Sigma_i + \Sigma_j}{2}\right|^{-1/2} \mathcal{M}_{3/2}\!\left(\sqrt{Q_{ij}}\right)$$

Regularised dimensionless variogram bandwidths stand at $\tau_1 = 1,5$ and $\tau_2 = 2,775$, with an effective short range spanning 71,04 km across all horizons (Table \ref{tab:kriging-scythian}). The model incorporates five biophysical covariates: habitable land fraction ($\beta_{\text{hab}} = 0,2159$ in Iron Age, $0,2222$ in Classical antiquity), natural vegetative productivity ($\beta_{\text{nat}} = 0,01$), ecozone suitability ($\beta_{\text{eco}} = 0,1093$), fluvial proximity decay ($\beta_{\text{fluvial}} = 0,1081$), and coastal/lacustrine proximity ($\beta_{\text{coastal}} = 0,1074$). Documented settlement cores from 917 catalogued sites condition local density surfaces, with urban buffers applied to preserve rural and pastoral baselines [@Franklin2023Archaeolog; @BETTS2016Akchakhan].

# Testing and Validation

## Regional Trajectory Reconciliation

Reconciliation confirms exact parity between territorial totals and regional aggregates across all seven historical benchmarks from 1000BC to 500AD. Table \ref{tab:validation-scythian} presents the longitudinal demographic trajectory decomposed into three macro-regional groupings: the Southern Oasis Core (Parthia-Margiana, Northern Bactria and Sogdiana), the Northern Oasis and Syr Darya (Khwarazm, Dayuan Ferghana and Kangju Chach), and the Steppe and Highland Pastoralists (Pamir, Semirechye, Massagetae and Tasmola).

# Results

## Early Iron Age Pastoral and Satrapal Emergence (1000BC to 500BC)

Between 1000BC and 500BC, Central Asia evolved from decentralised Bronze Age agro-pastoral communities into organised Saka nomadic confederations and Achaemenid imperial satrapies (Figure \ref{fig:traj-scythian}) [@Librado2024Widespread; @Morris2021Economic]. In 1000BC, domain population stood at 1,45M people, including 667k across the southern oases, 391,5k in northern oases and 391,5k across the steppes (Table \ref{tab:regions-scythian}).

<figure class="crd-figure-block" id="fig:traj-scythian">
<img class="crd-figure-img" src="/artefacts/project_saray/1.0-scythian-saka-and-classical-oasis-states/fig2_scythian_saka_and_classical_oasis_states_trajectory.png" alt="fig:traj-scythian" loading="lazy" />
<figcaption class="crd-caption"><span class="crd-caption-label">Figure 2.</span> Demographic trajectory of Central Asian oasis states and pastoral confederations from 1000BC to 500AD across nine subregions.</figcaption>
</figure>

Under Achaemenid Persian administrative unification after 530BC, total population grew by 51,7% to reach 2,2M in 500BC [@Morris2023Economic; @Grenet2025Histoire]. Imperial peace and state-sponsored canal engineering fostered major growth in Sogdiana, which expanded from 304,5k in 1000BC to 462k in 500BC (densities rising from 2,47 to 3,75 persons per km²), while Northern Bactria grew from 174k to 264k [@MirMakhamad2024Agricultur; @Sanahuja2020Historiogr]. Parthia and Margiana climbed from 188,5k to 286k, sustained by the expansion of the Murghab delta canal systems and the fortification of Merv (Gyaur Kala) [@Dhawi2024Oasis]. 

In Classical Khwarazm, population expanded from 145k to 220k, accompanied by the construction of monumental mudbrick fortresses and palaces such as Akchakhan-kala, which celebrated local royal lineages under Achaemenid suzerainty [@BETTS2016Akchakhan]. Steppe pastoral groups flourished concurrently: the Tasmola culture across central Kazakhstan and the Massagetae along the trans-Caspian steppe grew from 145k and 87k to 220k and 132k respectively, benefiting from active cross-border trade in horses, copper and livestock [@Librado2024Widespread; @Cinar2026Kazakh].

<figure class="crd-figure-block" id="fig:density-scythian">
<img class="crd-figure-img" src="/artefacts/project_saray/1.0-scythian-saka-and-classical-oasis-states/fig3_scythian_saka_and_classical_oasis_states_density.png" alt="fig:density-scythian" loading="lazy" />
<figcaption class="crd-caption"><span class="crd-caption-label">Figure 3.</span> Continuous kriged population density surface and territorial demographic densities across Central Asia at the Classical Kushan apex.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Hellenistic Urban Expansion and Agricultural Intensification (500BC to 200BC)

The Hellenistic period (330BC to 130BC) ushered in a wave of Mediterranean-style urbanism, monetised market exchange and agricultural diversification (Figure \ref{fig:density-scythian}) [@Sanahuja2020Historiogr; @Morris2021Economicb]. Domain population expanded from 2,2M in 500BC to 2,75M in 200BC (Table \ref{tab:regions-scythian}).

The Greco-Bactrian Kingdom established fortified polis settlements equipped with stone administrative archives, gymnasia and mints, lifting Northern Bactrian population to 330k (2,53 persons per km²) in 200BC [@Sanahuja2020Historiogr; @Francfort2020Quelques]. Sites such as Old Termez and Takht-i Sangin controlled strategic crossings of the Oxus, funnelling Indian ivory, semi-precious stones and Chinese silk into the Mediterranean basin [@Sanahuja2020Historiogr; @Franklin2023Archaeolog]. In Margiana and Parthia, the Seleucids and early Arsacids expanded Antiochia Margiana (Merv) and Parthaunisa (Nisa), elevating regional headcounts to 357,5k [@Morris2021Economic; @Morris2023Political].

Sogdiana remained the economic engine of Central Asia, expanding to 577,5k people in 200BC [@MirMakhamad2024Agricultur]. Marakanda (Samarkand) grew into a formidable walled city, supported by high-yielding wheat, barley and grape cultivation along the middle Zeravshan [@MirMakhamad2024Agricultur; @MirMakhamad2023Food]. Dayuan Ferghana and Kangju Chach reached 467,5k, supported by intensive irrigation agriculture and celebrated horse-breeding pastures [@Zhang2023Characteri].

## The Classical Kushan-Parthian Imperial Zenith (200BC to 200AD)

Between 200BC and 200AD, Central Asia attained its pre-modern demographic zenith under the Kushan Empire, Arsacid Parthian Margiana, Classical Khwarazm and the Kangju confederation (Table \ref{tab:regions-scythian}) [@Morris2021Economic; @Morris2023Political]. Total domain population expanded from 2,75M in 200BC to 3,45M in 1AD and peaked at 3,75M in 200AD (Table \ref{tab:validation-scythian}).

Sogdiana formed the demographic apex of the domain, supporting 787,5k inhabitants (6,38 persons per km²) across its fertile alluvial corridors (Table \ref{tab:density-scythian}) [@MirMakhamad2024Agricultur]. Major urban nucleations flourished at Samarkand (38.000 residents in 200AD), Bukhara (26.000), Erkurgan (18.000), Paykand (12.000) and Shahrisabz (15.000) [@Anon2022Some; @Armaroli2026Tracing]. Archaeobotanical data confirm the widespread cultivation of broomcorn and foxtail millet, free-threshing wheat, naked barley, lentils, melons, peaches and grapes, while proteomic and isotopic analyses at Kafir Kala reveal sophisticated pastoral management, seasonal transhumance and cattle-horse draft labour [@MirMakhamad2024Agricultur; @Armaroli2026Tracing; @Peters2024Archaeolog].

In Northern Bactria (Tokharistan), Kushan imperial patronage supported 450k inhabitants (3,45 persons per km²), anchored by Old Termez (38.000 peak residents), Dalverzin-Tepe (15.000) and Takht-i Sangin [@Morris2021Economic; @Sanahuja2020Historiogr]. Dalverzin-Tepe expanded into a lavish urban centre boasting palatial residences, Buddhist shrines, terra-cotta sculpture workshops and buried hoards of gold ornaments [@Morris2021Economic; @Francfort2020Quelques]. 

In Dayuan Ferghana and Kangju Chach, population peaked at 637,5k people, sustained by intensive canal irrigation along the Syr Darya and bustling transit markets at Kanka (22.000 residents), Tashkent (14.000) and Otrar (12.000) [@Zhang2023Characteri; @Cinar2026Kazakh]. Parthian Margiana supported 487,5k people, with Merv housing 55.000 residents within its fortified mudbrick ramparts, surrounded by lush vineyards, orchards and industrial ceramic quarters [@Morris2021Economic; @Dhawi2024Oasis]. Classical Khwarazm reached 375k people, governed from the grand palatial complex of Toprak-Kala (12.000 residents) and Kunya-Urgench (18.000 residents) [@BETTS2016Akchakhan].

## Late Antique Transformation, Nomadic Dispersals and Hephthalite Reconfiguration (200AD to 500AD)

The third and fourth centuries AD brought political fragmentation, ecological stress and nomadic incursions from the Eurasian steppe [@Grenet2025Histoire; @Morris2023Political]. The collapse of the Kushan Empire following Sasanian Persian campaigns under Ardashir I and Shapur I fragmented Tokharistan into Sasanian vassal principalities (Kushano-Sasanians) [@Morris2023Political; @Grenet2025Histoire]. Concurrently, climatic drying across the northern steppes propelled Chionite, Kidarite and early Hunnic nomadic groups southward into Transoxiana and Bactria [@Grenet2025Histoire; @SENGUL2024Origin].

These disruptions depressed trade and caused localized canal decay, causing domain population to contract by 10,7% from 3,75M in 200AD to 3,35M in 350AD (Table \ref{tab:validation-scythian}) [@Morris2021Economic; @Grenet2025Histoire]. Sogdiana declined from 787,5k to 703,5k, Northern Bactria fell from 450k to 402k, and Margiana contracted from 487,5k to 435,5k [@Morris2021Economic; @MirMakhamad2024Agricultur].

By the late fifth century, the rise of the Hephthalite Empire (White Huns) restored political stability and administrative coherence across Central Asia [@Grenet2025Histoire; @Franklin2023Archaeolog]. Establishing their primary capitals at Kunduz, Termez and Balkh, the Hephthalites subjugated the Sasanians, extracted massive tribute in silver drachms, and protected transnational caravan commerce [@Grenet2025Histoire; @Franklin2023Archaeolog]. 

Sogdian merchant diaspora networks expanded vigorously across the Tarim Basin into Northern Wei and Liang China, founding trade colonies at Dunhuang, Turfan, Chang'an and Luoyang [@Franklin2023Archaeolog; @Zhang2023Characteri; @Wang2022Revealing]. This mercantile renaissance stimulated domestic agricultural recovery along the Zeravshan and Syr Darya, lifting domain population to 3,55M by 500AD (Table \ref{tab:regions-scythian}) [@MirMakhamad2024Agricultur; @Franklin2023Archaeolog]. Sogdiana rebounded to 745,5k people, Ferghana-Chach rose to 603,5k, and Margiana reached 461,5k, establishing the demographic foundation for the early mediaeval Islamic era [@MirMakhamad2023Food; @Anon2022Some].

## Classical Oasis Settlement Hierarchy

The 917 settlements catalogued across the nine territories demonstrate a pronounced urban hierarchy shaped by imperial capitals, regional oasis nodes and fortified frontier outposts [@Sanahuja2020Historiogr; @BETTS2016Akchakhan; @Morris2021Economic]:

1. Merv (Antiochia Margiana/Gyaur Kala): The foremost urban centre of the domain, situated at the terminus of the Murghab delta in southern Turkmenistan, sustaining an estimated 60.000 residents in 500AD (55.000 in 200AD) within massive mudbrick defensive walls enclosing over 340 hectares of residential, administrative and industrial quarters [@Morris2021Economic; @Dhawi2024Oasis].
2. Samarkand (Afrasiab/Marakanda): The royal capital of Sogdiana, commanding the middle Zeravshan alluvial plain, housing 45.000 residents in 500AD (38.000 in 200AD) across a naturally defended loess plateau fortified by multi-tiered ramparts and palaces [@Anon2022Some; @Armaroli2026Tracing].
3. Old Termez (Demetrias/Tarmita): The pre-eminent port and crossing hub of the upper Oxus in Northern Bactria, sustaining 38.000 residents in 200AD within a vast fortified complex containing Greco-Bactrian civil architecture, Kushan palatial quarters and prominent Buddhist monastic complexes at Kara-Tepe and Fayaz-Tepe [@Sanahuja2020Historiogr; @Morris2021Economic].
4. Bukhara (Numijkat): The western anchor of the lower Zeravshan oasis, housing 35.000 residents in 500AD (26.000 in 200AD), operating as a crucial caravanserai nexus linking Transoxiana with Khwarazm and Iran [@MirMakhamad2023Food; @Armaroli2026Tracing].
5. Old Nisa (Mithradatkert): The royal fortress and ceremonial capital of the early Arsacid Parthian kings along the Kopet Dag piedmont, sustaining 24.000 residents in 1AD, featuring grand columned halls, royal wine cellars and carved ivory rhytons [@Morris2021Economic; @Morris2023Political].
6. Tashkent (Chach/Ming Uruk): The principal urban hub of the Chirchiq river basin, sustaining 22.000 residents in 500AD [@Zhang2023Characteri].
7. Kunya-Urgench (Gurganj): The premier emporium of northern Khwarazm, sustaining 22.000 residents in 500AD (18.000 in 200AD) [@BETTS2016Akchakhan].
8. Khujand (Alexandria Eschate): Guarding the western entrance to the Ferghana Valley along the Syr Darya, housing 22.000 residents in 500AD [@Sanahuja2020Historiogr].
9. Akhsikent: The ancient fortified capital of the Ferghana Valley, sustaining 22.000 residents in 500AD [@Zhang2023Characteri].
10. Kanka: The primary fortified urban stronghold of the Kangju confederation in the Tashkent oasis, sustaining 22.000 residents in 200AD within triple concentric mudbrick walls [@Zhang2023Characteri; @Anon2026].
11. Erkurgan: The major classical city of the Qashqadarya oasis (southern Sogdiana), sustaining 18.000 residents in 200AD with extensive ceramic and metallurgical quarters [@Morris2021Economic].
12. Shahrisabz (Kesh): Anchoring the upper Qashqadarya basin with 15.000 residents in 200AD [@Anon2022Some].
13. Dalverzin-Tepe: The premier Kushan administrative and monastic centre in the Surkhandarya valley, housing 15.000 residents in 200AD [@Morris2021Economic; @Francfort2020Quelques].

## Analytical Caveats and Taphonomic Preservation

Three methodological caveats condition the precision of this demographic reconstruction. First, differential taphonomic preservation and alluvial sedimentation obscure early settlement horizons [@Franklin2023Archaeolog; @MirMakhamad2024Agricultur]. In active river valleys such as the Zeravshan and Syr Darya, dynamic river channel avulsion and intensive agricultural silting have buried early Iron Age and Hellenistic levels beneath several metres of sediment, rendering early occupation phases less visible than surface-exposed late antique and mediaeval ruins [@MirMakhamad2024Agricultur; @Dhawi2024Oasis].

Second, architectural contemporaneity across sprawling mudbrick tell settlements introduces an uncertainty envelope estimated at $\pm 15\%$ to $\pm 20\%$ [@Morris2021Economic; @BETTS2016Akchakhan]. While surface mudbrick walls may appear contemporary across an excavation trench, micro-stratigraphic analyses reveal sequential room abandonments, domestic re-allocations and seasonal workshop use [@BETTS2016Akchakhan; @Armaroli2026Tracing]. 

Third, the ephemeral nature of mobile pastoral encampments leads to systemic under-representation in standard settlement gazetteers [@Librado2024Widespread; @Zairova2026Phenomenon]. Unlike sedentary mudbrick towns, mobile Saka, Massagetae and Wusun communities occupied seasonal tent camps leaving minimal permanent architectural debris [@Zairova2026Phenomenon; @Namen2025Human]. To prevent under-counting, this study anchors pastoral population floors through carrying-capacity estimates of pasture biomass, waterhole distributions and mortuary kurgan densities [@Librado2024Widespread; @SENGUL2024Origin; @Anon2026].
